book: 118 - Scott Adams and Philosophy - A Hole in the Fabric of Reality
essays: 1. How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Tolerate the Master Persuader Hypothesis
2. Persuade Me Once, Shame on You . .
3. How I Could Have Made Hillary President
5. The Serious Point of Scott’s Humor
8. Is It a Fact that Facts Don’t Matter
12. Dilbert Is an Asshole and That’s Why He’ll Never Be Happy and Nobody Loves Him
18. Scott Adams and the Pinocchio Fallacy
samples: The editors' introduction sets up the book: in 2016 Scott Adams, a left-leaning Mensa member trained in hypnosis, predicted a 98-percent Trump landslide on the ground that Trump is a rare Master Persuader whose outrageous statements were calibrated weapons-grade persuasion aimed at irrational, emotion-driven voters who rationalize after the fact, and that the victory would rip a hole in the fabric of reality, producing cognitive dissonance and mass hysteria among Hillary supporters. It then profiles Adams's path from bank teller and 4 a.m. cartoonist at Pacific Bell to Dilbert creator, business guru (The Dilbert Principle and the Logitech gibberish mission-statement prank in a false mustache), fiction writer (God's Debris, The Religion War), talent-stack theorist of How to Fail at Almost Everything and Still Win Big, and author of Win Bigly, framing the volume as philosophy's examination of this gadfly.

Wolfe reads Adams's Master Persuader hypothesis through the ancient quarrel between Socrates and the Sophists: Derren Brown's deflation of hypnosis into one personality dominating another leads to Gorgias's Encomium of Helen, where persuasive words are magic spells that steal free will, and to Plato's Gorgias, where Socrates condemns rhetoric as cookery and cosmetics that flatter the ignorant while his disciple Polus covets its tyrannical power. On this mapping Trump's plain-talk style is simply Aristotle's available means of persuasion for a particular audience, and Adams is mostly a Sophist who treats words as programming code for moist robots, though he keeps a Socratic sliver in his stated aim of exposing readers to different ideas rather than converting them. Wolfe closes by refusing both readings of Adams as pro-Trump troll or alt-right hero, urging each side to see how persuasion actually worked on them.

Greene dismantles both phases of Adams's case that Trump is a Master Persuader. The trait-list phase (opening with big demands, the Intentional Wrongness Persuasion Play, never apologizing, exuding confidence, recruiting the reciprocity instinct, and the talent stack) fails because doing what master persuaders do is not being one, by the Tom Brady versus Archie Manning point that we never define good quarterbacks by wins alone and by the Kantian thought that an act must be done for the right reason. The reality phase borrows Plato, Hume, and Kant to deny us access to an objective world, but the chapter replies that the experts' predictive failures illustrate Hume's problem of induction rather than proving there are no facts, notes Adams even misreads Plato, and observes that nothing links the Persuasion Filter's one success to Trump's skills rather than to a one-off political climate.

Taking Adams at his word that persuasion is learnable technique, Steele dissects Trump's linguistic kill shots (Low-energy Jeb, Crooked Hillary, Lyin' Ted, Pocahontas) as visual, confirmation-bias-proof forever names that killed Jeb Bush's candidacy in half a second, and contrasts the Clinton campaign's committee flops (Donald Duck, Dangerous Donald, Drumpf, and slogans like Love Trumps Hate and Stronger Together). He then practices what Adams preaches by drafting his own kill shot, The Don, a mafia frame built on offers that cannot be refused, omerta, and sleeping with the fishes, plus the slogan A Win-Win for America, engineered for positive repetition and the slightly-off meaning Adams calls intentional wrongness, concluding the election was winnable with commonsense marketing touches. An Orwell aside about whose victory a wartime poster really celebrates supplies the only classical rhetoric on display.

Karavitis finds a Hegelian dialectic in the three-panel Dilbert strip (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) delivered through irony, then tests that irony against philosophy: Socrates' feigned-ignorance questioning that leaves interlocutors in aporia, Hegel's complaint that irony is vanity withdrawing from objective reality, and Kierkegaard's dissertation on the concept of irony plus Either/Or, where irony is the bridge from the aesthetic to the ethical life. The punchline is that after nearly three decades of Dilbert the white-collar workplace has not changed, so readers who feel superior to their bosses and co-workers have taken the vain, narcissistic, aesthetic reading Hegel warned against, making the joke a scoundrelly way of avoiding responsibility. A Leo Strauss aside casts Adams as an esoteric writer whose irony preserves him from the powerful.

Guerra and Barkman argue that Dilbert's humor is doing serious philosophical work: strips like the Pointy-Haired Boss's scheme to strip app users of free will, rebranded by Dilbert as marketing, distill manipulative corporate practice to its absurd essential core, and humor serves as a logical tool that, when it preserves the target's integrity rather than straw-manning it, exposes the equivocation in earnest arguments about getting something from nothing. They ground the practice in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, where wittiness is the virtuous mean between the vices of buffoonery and boorishness, read Adams's catalogue of failures and his luck-first, passion-is-bullshit account of success as a Socratic acknowledgment of ignorance that deflates the American Dream, and treat Win Bigly's persuasion lessons (visuals, repetition, intentional mistakes, the Hitler counterexample) as further proof that Adams has the virtue of wit.

book: 119 - Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!
essays: 1. Dream Investigations of Tree House Operations
5. Albert Among the Chowder-Head Yokels and Blithering Hayseeds
7. The Art of Playing Along with Dancing Little People
8. I Sure Feel Uncomfortable Being in This Situation with You
9. My Dharma Is the Road that Never Ends
10. The Miss Twin Peaks Award Goes To . .
12. It’s Not About BOB—It Never Was
14. Diane, I Am Now Upside Down
samples: Argues that Twin Peaks is a critique of the scientism of TV crime procedurals: real murder investigation mixes induction, intuition, and luck with science rather than delivering deductive certainty. It contrasts Albert's forensic confidence (undermined by the 2016 PCAST report showing bite-mark, fingerprint, gun, and footwear matching fail scientific standards) with Cooper's openly non-scientific methods — the Tibetan rock-throwing test in "Zen, or the Skill to Catch a Killer," the Giant's clues, and his "Arbitrary Law" list of "bureau guidelines, deductive technique, Tibetan method, instinct, and luck ... magic." Truman's collaborative, unscientific policing completes the picture that solving Laura's murder takes every kind of inquiry, including magic. The upshot is a warning to jurors and citizens not to treat police conclusions as established like physics.

Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.

Applies Freud's Madonna-whore complex — "where such men love, they have no desire, and where they desire, they cannot love" — to Laura Palmer's split between homecoming queen/Meals on Wheels volunteer and cocaine-prostitute, arguing the contradiction exists only in a mindset that forces women into two poles, which BOB weaponizes with his "dirty and sleazy" refrain. The chapter surveys explanations of the complex (incest fear, paternity anxiety, alpha-male identity visible in Leo and Jacques), and then indicts the Fireman as a feminist "nice guy": his Part 8 creation of Laura as a golden orb of purity sent to redeem the world of the Bomb is the ultimate Madonna role, a Christ-like burden that is what makes her the target BOB must debase. Even her friends' names — Maddie and Donna — spell Madonna.

A chapter-length epistemology tutorial delivered as Cooper's tapes to Diane, applying the justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge to his investigation. An Invitation to Love example (Chet's Ouija board actually guided by Jade's ghost) distinguishes internalist justification from externalist/reliabilist justification — a belief formed by a truth-conducive process can be justified even when the believer lacks reasons — and Cooper then earns internal justification by treating his dreams and visions as a hypothesis that yields testable predictions: "sometimes her arms bend back" matches Albert's autopsy, and the Giant's three pronouncements (man in a smiling bag, the owls are not what they seem, without chemicals he points) are confirmed by Jacques' hanging body bag, Major Briggs' deep-space transmission, and MIKE emerging off his haloperidol. The chapter cautions against confirming vague prophecies like bunny-shaped clouds, concluding Cooper becomes a truly "Special Epistemic Agent."

Argues that Albert Rosenfield embodies Kant's categorical imperative: his refusal to soften his autopsy demands or lie to spare feelings is fidelity to universalizable maxims, and his insistence that Sheriff Truman be charged for punching him treats punishment as respect for a rational agent's autonomy. The chapter walks through maxims, the universalizability test applied to Gordon Cole's possibly faked deafness and FBI lying, hypothetical versus categorical imperatives (Cooper may always want Norma's cherry pie, but morality trumps want), and the formula of humanity — Ben Horne's use of One-Eyed Jack's women as mere means is the counterexample, while Albert's insults paradoxically honor Truman's rational agency. Albert's arc to "I love you, Sheriff Truman" and his gentler Season Two and The Return self shows a Kantian who integrates classical reason with romantic feeling.

Argues that asking "what does it mean?" of Twin Peaks is the wrong question, because Lynch builds the show out of aesthetically incomplete material. Kant's "purposiveness without purpose" and the free play of understanding and imagination explain the opening credits' waterfalls, pines, and mill blades, while Russell's incomplete symbols ("the present king of France is bald") model the swaying traffic light and Harriet's "full blossom of the evening," and Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence applies to Black Lodge clues like "the man in the smiling bag" and the Arm's whoops, which support many consistent but unprovable interpretations. Susanne Langer's account of film as a dream-like virtual present, capped by Part 8's atomic-bomb sequence, grounds the claim that Lynch means viewers to complete the meaning themselves.

essays: 4. To Be or Not to Be Perfect
5. The Funny Thing about Being Yourself
9. Girls Just Wanna Have Mediated Fun
12. Putting the Fun Back in Non-refundable
14. Five Stereotypes that Sustain Grape Zones
15. Are There Certain Things We Should Not Talk About
samples: Argues that Schumer's self-deprecating and gallows humor succeeds when it models transcendence, connection, and acceptance, drawing on Freud's relief theory of laughter as a discharge of repressed energy. Atkinson reads the Trainwreck funeral scene where Amy turns on Aaron after her father's burial, plus the memoir's 'grape' and clam-chowder consent jokes, as gallows humor inviting audiences to laugh both at and with her. She contrasts the failing Snatched tapeworm and flirting scenes, which degrade Emily rather than showing her overcoming her circumstances, and frames the whole practice as humility rather than humiliation.

Uses the superiority theory of humor to ask who the butt of a self-deprecating joke really is. Alloy first worries that jokes like 'I've only been with four people' reaffirm the standards behind slut-shaming and body-shaming, then argues that good self-deprecation makes the shaming standard itself the butt, reading 'Last Fuckable Day' and the '12 Angry Men Inside Amy Schumer' jury sketch as ridiculing the chastity, sobriety, and thinness norms imposed on women. That is why Schumer is 'brave': not for the underwear photo, but for mocking those who called it brave.

Weighs psychological egoism, the thesis that every action is ultimately self-interested, against apparent altruism through Schumer's cluelessly selfish characters: the 'Cancer Excuse' sketch where Amy exploits Tig Notaro's diagnosis, God's dismay at her in 'Herpes Scare', and Emily Middleton guilt-tripping her mother into an Ecuador trip in Snatched. Arp deploys Adam Smith's Chinese-earthquake passage from The Theory of Moral Sentiments and Rachels's Lincoln piglets story before rejecting the argument for ethical egoism on is-ought and coherence grounds, concluding Schumer's selfish jerks are comic negative examples of how not to live.

Asks whether chasing externally imposed perfection is worthwhile and reads Schumer's comedy as an invitation to drop society's 'suggested' standards, from the impossible pre-sex grooming ritual of 'Sex Prep' to the pole-dancing hypocrisy of 'Judging Strippers'. Flieswasser tests three models of human perfection: the Platonic and Cartesian privileging of mind over body, monotheistic modesty, and Aristotle's telos as an individual purpose. She then lands on the Japanese aesthetics of wabi-sabi and kintsugi, where broken pieces are rejoined into something more beautiful, as the truest picture of Schumer's self-acceptance.

Reads Schumer's comedy as Nietzschean self-creation: like the tightrope walker over the abyss she confronts who she is, says 'Yes' to life in the spirit of the eternal recurrence and amor fati, and 'gives style' to her character by wearing mistakes as badges of honor, notably reclaiming her paparazzi photos in the Leather Special. Balke then casts her as Rorty's ironist, whose continual burning of old material keeps her free of a 'final vocabulary' in a contingent world, with 'Amy Goes Deep' doing the Rortian work of testing herself against others. He closes with George Herbert Mead's account of a self formed through social interaction with significant others.

Distinguishes public intellectuals like Chomsky, who deliver their own conclusions, from public philosophers who get audiences thinking for themselves, and argues Schumer is the latter. Her memoir claim that she has 'no wisdom to offer' is set beside the Socratic ignorance of Plato's Apology, where wisdom is worth nothing. Sketches like 'Football Town Nights', whose coach condemns rape only to praise violent domination, and 'The Trial of Bill Cosby' withhold conclusions and force viewers to work out for themselves the links between football and rape culture, or between un-conflicted entertainment and justice.

book: 121 - The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit
essays: 6. In a Mirror Is Our Image
7. Loss of Memory, Loss of Me
12. The Twilight Zone on Our Doorstep
15. The Twists and Turns of Second Chances
17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone
18. War Means Fighting and Fighting Includes Philosophizing
samples: The editors introduce the volume with Nietzsche's line about finding only 'apes of our ideal': TZ episodes dangle wishes (rejuvenated husbands, fallout shelters, Henry Bemis's time to read) that fate twists into cosmic jokes, so we laugh at what we fail to be. They cast Rod Serling as a reincarnation of Socrates, the gadfly of Athens, whose episodes work as thought experiments exposing expert promises as tricks, and set 'The Hunt' against this cynicism — the faithful dog Rip smells the Devil's gate so the old man reaches Heaven. The tension between our ideals and human frailty, they argue, is what made the show philosophical television.

Rard applies David Lewis's definition of time travel — a discrepancy between the journey's duration and externally elapsed time — to argue that the suspended-animation gold thieves of 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' never time-traveled, while Flight Lieutenant Decker in 'Last Flight' does, creating a consistent causal loop in which his 1959 knowledge that he saved Mackaye is what sends him back to 1917 to save him. She then reads 'No Time Like the Past' as enacting the impossibility of changing the past: Paul Driscoll's attempt to shoot Hitler is thwarted by a maid and SS officers exactly as Lewis's 'bananas peel' account predicts, and his retreat to 1881 Homeville makes him the unwitting cause of the very schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent — his foreknowledge, not fate, was always the cause.

Scalambrino argues the Twilight Zone is a televised expression of Breton's surrealism, starting from Descartes: the cogito and the mind–body problem made reason the measure of the 'clear and distinct,' and surrealism seeks to unbind the imagination from exactly that rational leash. He reads 'A World of His Own' as surrealist automatic writing, 'The Mirror' as Dalí's paranoiac-critical method, and Freud's psychoanalysis as both allied with and (following Adorno's diagnosis of the movement's death) too restrictive for surrealism's project. Episodes like 'Shadow Play' (a man who dreams the world), 'The Shelter,' 'The Lonely,' and 'A Stop at Willoughby' provoke the uncanny — the strangely familiar — in viewers, which is where the Zone is located.

Pichanick reads 'Time Enough at Last' as a tragic dilemma: Henry Bemis's wish to own his time, away from the bank president's productivity, his wife's social demands, and the 'unrelenting clock,' is granted by a nuclear blast that turns solitude into a monotonous prison driving him to attempted suicide, until the library restores meaning, identity, and freedom. The shattered glasses then reveal his 'short-sightedness': his literal vision always depended on other people and on a piece of technology, so the possibility of meaning itself was socially and technologically manufactured. The episode's brilliance, he argues, is refusing to choose between accepting the social world's limits on our freedom and withdrawing from it — it only shows that misanthropic withdrawal is self-destruction.

Hooke frames the volume through Levinas's claim that the face presents itself from a dimension of transcendence, with Kierkegaard's Abraham, Sartre's existential look, and Beauvoir's faces of the elderly and the second sex in the background, plus Lingis on trust. He shows how TZ masks its deadliest figures with trusted faces — Robert Redford as Death in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's avuncular Pip revealing 'This is the other place!' in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' the witch of 'Jess-Belle,' the gentle Kanamits whose book turns out to be a cookbook — so that proof of trust is nearly impossible and the show has us laughing with the Devil. The Turing test is applied to Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' (clearly in love 'regardless of the organs or hardware beneath'), the slot machine of 'The Fever,' and the aged couple of 'The Trade-Ins,' whose faces silently recognize a lost shared life.

Clayman uses 'The Lonely' as a case study for whether Corry's love for the robot Alicia is true love, classifying it through C.S. Lewis's four loves (charity, affection, friendship, Eros) and their gift-, need-, and appreciative-love qualities. He deploys Peirce's pragmatic maxim to read the meaning of 'truly loving' off its practical effects, answers the objection that a machine beloved involves prejudice with Singer's speciesism, and borrows Kendall Walton's 'Fearing Fictions' to explain how Corry, knowing Alicia is a machine, 'becomes fictional' and role-plays a believer — concluding he showed affection and friendship born of loneliness, not Eros, since he would not sacrifice his place on the ship for her.

book: 122 - Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown
essays: The Ethics of Pretending to Be a Cowboy
“Do you even know where you are ”
“I Always Felt this Place was Missing a Real Villain. Hence, My Humble Contribution.”
From Westworld to the World Outside and Back
Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person
Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous
Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful
Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve
“When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”
Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”
Westworld and the Power of Catharsis
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Westworld forces viewers to take sides not just between humans and hosts but on what we mean by 'choice' itself, since Dolores's line 'I choose to see the beauty' only makes sense against an account of choosing that the show destabilizes. It frames the volume's guiding question — what it is to be human when hosts and humans are indistinguishable — via Ford's 'you're only human, after all.' It closes with a tribute to the late co-editor Susanne Foster, invoking Cora Diamond on reality's resistance to our thinking and Aristotle's claim that wonder and astonishment are what prompt us to try to understand.

Fallis tests successive definitions of pretense against Westworld cases — William and Logan playing bounty hunters, Ford's pretense that Bernard is human, Maeve hiding her awakening, Hector and Armistice playing dead — rejecting Austin-style intent-to-deceive because guests don't aim to fool anyone, and settling on Langland-Hassan's account that pretending is acting as if P while believing P is false. For deception, he argues the Cartesian evil-demon definition (making things appear otherwise) is too narrow, since Ford implanting Teddy's false Wyatt backstory deceives just as much by bypassing the host's agency. Ethically, he concludes via Kant that the staff wrong the hosts because deception interferes with autonomy, and that guests like William are culpable despite lacking deceptive intent, much like Walzer's commander who foresees civilian casualties.

Moll argues the park works as a grandiose role-playing game — a sandbox crossed with a LARP, with Ford and the directorial staff as Game Master — offering guests linear narratives with only the illusion of choice. Using MacIntyre's narrative unity of life and Bernard Williams's 'constraints of coherence,' he reads guest role-play as authoring a competing, parallel narrative of the self, so that William's discovery of his capacity for cruelty and transformation into the Man in Black exemplifies the park's violent, rule-mediated path to 'self-knowledge.' He ends by suggesting that the park's educative, transformative experience may be reserved not for the guests but for the hosts who produce it.

Arvan argues the entire series, lab included, literally takes place inside a videogame, citing physically impossible events (Teddy's bullets cannot hurt the Man in Black, William steps onto a moving train, workers appear instantly in a single unbroken shot) and NPC-like loops of the lab staff. He then claims Descartes had it backwards: whether we are in a dream, Spinoza's God's mind, or a simulation (Bostrom's hypothesis, extended by his own peer-to-peer variant that would explain quantum indeterminacy and relativity), to be simulated is still to be real. Via Chalmers-style structuralism, anything structured and functioning like a person is a person, so hosts who walk, talk, love, and suffer are persons — and the humans' rape, torture, and murder of them, like our treatment of Siri and Watson, is dehumanization on a par with slavery and the Holocaust.

Lyons applies Masahiro Mori's uncanny valley to the hosts, whose near-human faces and movements turn initial revulsion into empathy — doubling it because the hosts suffer under programming humans would resist. She then argues, through Aristotle's virtue and vice and Nietzsche's discipline of great suffering, that hosts like Maeve (returning for her daughter) and Dolores ('I choose to see the beauty') display more 'human excellence' than the guests: Logan's hand-stabbing cruelty is mere vice and the Man in Black's scalping sadism falls under Aristotle's bestial. Humanity, she concludes, is a way of behaving rather than a way of being, and Mori's hope that robots may carry buddha-nature completes the title's reversal of machine and god.

Eberl asks whether living out Sizemore-style fantasies can reveal or only corrode character: applying Aristotle's account of virtues and vices as habituated dispositions, he argues William's three decades in the park habituated the vices that made him the Man in Black — the park reveals rather than suspends the self — while cruelty toward humanlike hosts hardens us toward people, as Aquinas and Kant warn about kindness to animals. Against Ford's claim that humans are wantons in tight loops, Maeve's editing of her own code after learning her escape was scripted makes her a Frankfurtian person who aligns first-order desires with second-order volitions, grounding her narrative identity and personhood. William too attains personhood by actualizing a second-order desire for a different life, with the hosts' free fight back evoking Nietzsche's will to power and Nozick's point that we want to actually do things, not merely experience them.

book: 123 - The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own
essays: 1. A Great Darkness Filled with Echoes
2. Dystopia from a Woman’s Point of View
8. From the Handmaid’s Tale to the Handmaids’ Tale
9. A Rose by Any Other Brand
16. Who Is the Meanest of Them All
19. How Language Shapes Reality in Gilead
samples: The editor's introduction argues that The Handmaid's Tale disturbs us because it shows how tenuous our civil liberties are, so we must actively watch political events for warning signs. It insists that a woman's value is not fixed by her body, fertility, or attractiveness—Handmaids are treated as incubators and commodities—and that the caring work women do is a power, not a weakness. It closes on the lesson that facts, not politicians, control the narrative, ending with 'Nolite te bastardes carborundorum.'

De Vaul argues Gilead terrifies because social cycle theory structures it: every detail, from the Puritan wedding-night sheet to Stalin-style purges and the Nazi and residential-school seizure of children, already happened, so Gilead reads as speculative rather than science fiction. Atwood's three stated influences—Puritan New England, the 1980s religious right, and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four—show history cycling back, with June as the apolitical 'backlash' daughter her second-wave mother Holly and the activist Moira both predicted. The pattern repeats at small scale (June relives the former Offred's Scrabble-and-affair story, Omar's family suffers June's own fate) and in the Historical Notes, where Pieixoto strips Offred of authorship, proving 'the past is a great darkness, filled with echoes.'

Robison-Greene reads The Handmaid's Tale as Atwood's answer to Nineteen Eighty-Four—a dystopia 'from the female point of view'—comparing how both regimes suppress critical thought by banning women's reading, rewriting texts (the Marx slogan 'from each according to her ability' passed off as St. Paul), and manufacturing perpetual war. She deploys Nietzsche's 'monumental' abuse of history, Kierkegaard's leap of faith (Offred's three contradictory versions of Luke's fate), and doublethink to show that believing contradictions becomes both the regime's tool and the victim's survival strategy. The woman's lens adds that reducing women to reproductive function (Marthas, Aunts, Jezebels) thrives where thinking is suppressed, that Beauvoir's point about women's complicity in their oppression is embodied by the Aunts, and that Offred and Nick's affair, like Winston and Julia's, is the act of freedom the Party can never quite own.

Kolb reads Gilead through Arendt's The Human Condition and The Origins of Totalitarianism: when reproduction becomes the means of production, women's labor is targeted, forcing fertile women into Animal laborans status as 'national resources' while denying them the creative freedom of Homo faber. She traces the polis/oikos split from Aristotle through Puritan capitalism to show Gilead overcorrecting into Aunt Lydia's 'freedom from'—totalitarian control of birth legitimized by the Rachel and Bilhah story and a Pauline creation story. The chapter ends with the transitional generation's forgetting (Offred's cave-delusion with Nick evoking Plato's Allegory of the Cave, the Holocaust documentarian 'thinking about how not to think') and Ofglen's bomb, arguing that thoughtfulness and literacy, not violence, are the only hopes against totalitarianism.

Greene argues that the contemporary United States under Trump exhibits early Gilead-like symptoms, detailing five shared techniques: othering (the Aunts' stereotypes of pre-Gilead women vs. Trump on Mexicans and Muslims), separating children from parents (Handmaid births and seizure of Hannah vs. immigrant detention camps), gaslighting (Janine's 'her fault' Testifying vs. inauguration-crowd and Mueller claims), discrediting dissent (Gilead's ban on reading vs. 'fake news'), and lying (Gilead's founding promise of elections vs. thousands of false claims and 'alternative facts'). He grounds the danger in the correspondence theory of truth: once leaders detach belief from how the world actually is, society is a small step from Atwood's dystopia.

Hirschbein unravels the Genesis story of Abraham, Sarah, and Hagar as the script Gilead rereads to rationalize its 'misogynist parlors,' arguing that Gilead's exegesis is propaganda rather than scholarship—cherry-picking scripture that Nietzsche joked would appall the actual Jesus. He then spins the reader's moral compass: with Rorty's ironist he asks whether anyone initiated into Abraham's tribe or raised in Gilead can be blamed—are even Hitler and Commander Waterford products of their time?—and weighs Ofglen's suicide bombing of the Rachel and Leah Center against just war criteria of proportion, innocence, and chance of success. Finally, with Freud and Niebuhr, he suggests the Sons of Jacob built their surveillance state on a depraved view of human nature, so utopian schemes—Gilead included—are doomed from the founding.

book: 124 - Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know
essays: 3. Don’t Come Around Here, Mary Jane
4. Tom Petty and the Meaning of Life
8. Tom Petty Didn’t Really Need to Know
samples: Luke Dick argues Petty is the best American rock and roll ever produced because his simple songs distill the American everyperson: the person in Indianola longing to leave a crummy town, the arrival in Hollywood finding it a sham. He contrasts Petty's effortless accessibility with the density of Dylan and Springsteen, and identifies Petty's signature move as making futility fun, a smart-assed drawled defiance heard in "American Girl" and "Mary Jane's Last Dance." The foreword frames the whole volume as a communion of fans trying to understand Petty from another lens, warning that the chapters will be hard pressed to beat Petty's own simplicity.

Section introduction to the ethics chapters, framed by Petty’s October 2017 death: it argues his real achievement was working to be timeless — the shelved 1982 outtake “Keep a Little Soul” sounding native in 2018 — and that he “lived what he believed,” chasing dreams despite guaranteed heartache, refusing to explain his songs, and standing up to record-company executives. It closes by describing Petty’s political thought as “a deontology that puts duty to the fans first,” invokes Nietzsche as appreciating the gesture of turning the volume up rather than snoozing through the Reagan years, and sketches the volume’s five philosophical “buds”: epistemology, aesthetics, ontology, and two ethics chapters on the outcast and heartbroken as redeemable antiheroes of the everyday.

Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.

Crippen and Dixon treat the album Echo, written during Petty's divorce, heroin use and severe depression, as organized by crisis and reversion: its lyrics and productions compulsively echo earlier eras of his life, from 1950s TV westerns and his abusive father in "About to Give Out" to the Jeff Lynne years and Wildflowers in "Accused of Love" and "Echo." They invoke Freud and Lacan's psychoanalytic account of trauma repetition, where the past is relived in hope of a different outcome and sublimated into art. The album's sparse, energy-conserving repetition is then read through Nietzsche's will-to-power cycle, in which merely holding on is symptomatic of illness, yet the closing "One More Day, One More Night" and the album's very creation exemplify Nietzschean health as strength to expand against obstacles, since we possess art lest we perish of the truth.

Auxier narrates three moments of Petty's video era (1979 Damn the Torpedoes, 1985, 1993) through Bataille's "general economy": living beings reduced to things can only be redeemed by wasting, sacrifice and death, which explains why the band devouring Alice in "Don't Come Around Here No More" and the morgue assistant dressing, dancing with and floating out Kim Basinger's corpse in "Mary Jane's Last Dance" are creepy yet somehow ordered rather than gratuitous. He argues MTV inverted the economy of music judgment so images became the cart pulling the horse, and reads Petty's top-hat ringmaster and the recurring circles of the videos as the ring of the sacred and profane where the accursed share of excess energy is spent. Phenomenology of the "creepy" is his method for seeing what MTV shows us but we prefer not to know.

Innes reads Petty through The Birth of Tragedy: Petty fuses Dionysian frenzy (the Oakland Coliseum "Makin' Some Noise" crowd as communal creation) with Apollonian form, and his refusal of genres, synthesizers and the hit-factory gives life the creative meaning Nietzsche demands. Jeff Lynne and ELO are cast as the contemporary Wagner, Socratic and Apollonian producers of pleasant ditties like "Don't Bring Me Down" that lack access to tragedy. Petty's "Trailer" models Greek tragedy (impulse as hamartia foreclosing freedom), while his lawsuits against MCA and The Last DJ dramatize the tragic bind that free musical expression needs the very industry that restrains it.

13. Rick, Morty, and the Cure for Unhappiness

samples: The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.

Written in the voice of a non-C-137 Rick, the chapter argues that whether the Beth at the end of 'The ABCs of Beth' is a clone doesn't matter, because our reverence for 'the genuine article' (like the original US Constitution) is romantic packaging, and a functional clone is as good as the original. It tests Robert Nozick's experience machine, whose three objections supposedly show we value genuine reality intrinsically, against Rick's pragmatism of believing what is useful, and reads 'The Wedding Squanchers' (Rick turning himself in to the Federation) as proof that his family is both instrumentally and intrinsically valuable to him. Your answer to the clone question, it concludes, is a Rorschach test revealing what you place intrinsic value on.

The chapter argues Rick C-137 is already dead: the Brainalyzer body-hops in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' and the Operation Phoenix swap in 'Big Trouble in Little Sanchez' copy psychological states rather than transfer a consciousness, so each post-transfer Rick is a new psychological clone, exactly as in Parfit's Teletransporter. Building from Locke's memory theory of personal identity to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, it reads the dimension-hop in 'Rick Potion #9', the Morty voucher, and the ambiguous clone Beth of 'The Rickchurian Mortydate' as the show itself endorsing psychological continuity over numerical identity. What matters is that someone carries on Rick's desires and relationships, so nobody noticed the protagonist's death.

The chapter runs Bostrom's simulation argument against 'M. Night Shaym-Aliens!', where the Zigerions trap Rick in simulations-within-simulations to steal his concentrated dark matter formula, and reads their cheap shortcuts ('My man!' NPCs, human music, Jerry's Appley award) as the glitches and shadow-people Bostrom predicts. It presses the epistemological problem that any evidence for the simulation equally supports its denial, an underdetermination that devastates the theory, and traces the lineage of 'the real world isn't real' through Plato's summoners and allegory of the cave, Descartes's dream doubt, and Paley's design analogy (Morty as the beautiful machine), ending with the microverse battery of 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy': this is the universe we live in, so get used to it.

Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.

Framing Rick's massacre of the Council of Ricks in 'The Rickshank Rickdemption' as a crime-scene investigation, the chapter asks whether killing qualitatively identical Ricks is murder or suicide. It contrasts Leibniz's abstractionism (possible worlds as mere descriptions, pictured as the Palace of Fates in the Theodicy, allowing transworld identity via essential properties) with David Lewis's concretism/modal realism (all worlds really exist but are causally isolated, with world-bound individuals and counterpart theory instead of transworld identity). The show, it argues, is a modified concretism: portals let people interact across worlds, so Rick C-137 murdered distinct cosmic doppelgangers, not himself, as the interdimensional cable channels of 'Rixty Minutes' confirm.

essays: How to Make Something Strange Even Stranger
2. Can Anything Good Come from the Upside Down
4. The Slimy, Macabre, and Horrific in Stranger Things
5. Horror Appeals to Our Dual Nature
6. The Unique Horror of the Upside Down
7. The Mind Flayer through a Gnostic Lens
9. To Err Is Human, to Forget … Sublime
samples: Andrew Winters's introduction argues the show appeals both to those who lived the Eighties and those who wish they had: plastic, story-rich 1980s childhoods (D&D, bikes, walkie-talkies) versus a present of single-bit tweets, likes, and Instagram-filtered self-display where we look to others for confirmation instead of creating worlds together. It then previews the volume's essays on horror's appeal, whether monsters like Dart are all evil, friendship and civil disobedience, the Shadow Monster within ourselves, Will's possession and identity, nostalgia and forgetting, and Eleven's faith and heroism as a guide to meaningful living, closing with Hopper's 'Mornings are for coffee and contemplation.'

Holmes and Christensen read the #JusticeForBarb movement through Baudrillard's hyperreality: fans mobilized real activism for a fictional girl the show killed as a plot device (dragged by the Demogorgon while Nancy and Steve are upstairs), while real murdered women like Jamie Haggard got no hashtag, so fictional justice becomes 'more real than the real.' The show itself is a simulacrum assembled from 1980s movies (E.T., Poltergeist, Firestarter, The Goonies, Stand by Me) whose grid motif casts the series as a D&D gameboard the audience plays, and the chapter argues hyperreal power became real power when the Duffers gave Barb a Season Two funeral and apology from Hawkins Lab.

Kuzma maps Augustine's two cities onto the two Hawkinses: not two places but two mixed moral orientations in one world, since Will is literally 'right here' in the same house flipped upside down. Augustine's privation view of evil (evil as absence of good, a nougat-less Three Musketeers) explains how Dart can come from the 'evil' Upside Down yet love Dustin and let the party pass, while Brenner, from the right side up, is ruled by libido dominandi like the Mind Flayer and Dr. Owens proves Hawkins Lab is not automatically bad; it is how you act, not where you are from.

Puumala asks whether killing the Demogorgons is speciesist: Dart's pain response to light makes the demodogs sentient (Bentham's 'Can they suffer?'), giving them moral considerability, while the Mind Flayer may or may not be a moral agent and could even be a keystone species whose destruction collapses the Upside Down ecosystem. He tests whether demogorgons count as invasive species (they may be native to a causally connected mirror dimension), invokes Regan's lifeboat case to argue they must still lose out to humans in a conflict of interests, and ends with the uncomfortable thought that humans are themselves an invasive species turning Earth into an Upside Down, so Eleven closing the gate was compassionate conservation.

Nisley applies Noel Carroll's account of art-horror to the Demogorgon: categorically transgressive, interdimensional monsters provoke thought-based fear and disgust (the shed goop, the hazmat suits, Barb's blood in the pool), and it is precisely this disgust that makes our curiosity about the monster's origin and disclosure pleasurable. She traces Nancy's investigation from Jonathan's photograph to the bear trap, brings in Plato's Leontius story from the Republic and Kieran and Feagin on the grotesque to explain why we paradoxically delight in Barb's slime-covered corpse and Will coughing up a slug, and concludes that revulsion amplifies the fascination that keeps us watching.

Allaire and Gehring argue horror works on Kierkegaard's dual nature, the tug-of-war between finitude and infinitude that produces despair: the show's corporeal terrors (the Demogorgon's kills, Barb's decomposing body with a slug in its mouth, Will's tentacle) trigger the fear of mutilation and extinction, while the intelligent Shadow Monster shatters our sense of being unique, echoing Ernest Becker's claim that we build cultural 'armor' against mortality. Using Carroll's paradox of horror and Stephen King's three levels (revulsion, horror, terror), they contend we enjoy confronting these fears safely from the couch, with the Shadow Monster looming over the Snow Ball as an emblem of real horrors, from AIDS to 9/11, still to come.

book: 127 - Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World
essays: Philosophy and Reality in Blade Runner 2049
1. Do You Long for Having Your Heart Interlinked
4. The Aesthetics of Being a Person
5. A Replicant’s Guide to Becoming Human
6. You Don’t Need to Be Human to Have a Human Hand
10. Should Humans Dream of Designer Babies
13. Flow My Tears, Rick Deckard Said
15. The Phenomenology of Replicant Life and Death
19. And God Created Replicants in His Own Image
samples: Robin Bunce's introduction shows that the word 'real' is used in at least six different senses in 2049: Joshi's authentic, K's genuine (unimplanted) memories, Joi's natural-born 'real boy', Stelline's naturalistic 'real human responses', Mariette's physical, and Deckard's true. It argues the film makes reality an essentially contested concept, then maps how each contributor deploys a different sense of 'real', from Baudrillard's simulacra in the chapter on women and birth to socialist realism in the Wallace chapter.

Timothy Shanahan asks whether K and Joi's relationship counts as romance, sex, and love, using Locke's definition of a person as a thinking, reflective being to ask whether a programmed AI can love, and weighing Joi's programming against the determinism that may bind human lovers too. He reads the Joi-Mariette-K sex scene through Plato's Symposium myth of severed halves seeking union, substance dualism, and a Kant-inspired 'controlled hallucination' view of perception, concluding all sex is a person-to-person conscious connection through bodily intermediaries. Deckard's rejection of Wallace's replica Rachael is explained with a Mona Lisa forgery analogy: an indistinguishable copy still lacks the irreplaceable original person. The baseline question 'Do you long for having your heart interlinked?' frames love as the longing of lonely cells of awareness to connect.

Chris Lay argues Joi is a person. He raises Searle's objection that programs only simulate understanding and need the right biological 'stuff', then answers it: Joi apparently violates her 'everything you want her to be' programming, so her affection for K is authentic either way. Testing Joi against Locke's personhood criteria — rationality, sentience, and self-consciousness grounded in memory and in her self-sacrifice before Luv — he adds a Cartesian reading in which her transfers between console and emanator make her a disembodied soul, closer to Descartes's essence of the human than embodied replicants are. If a digital person like Joi would also fail the baseline, the wall separating kind would need a full societal reset.

Aron Ericson reads being 'real' in 2049 as being special: having an existence that is your own. Borrowing Stephen Mulhall's reading of the first film — life gets its meaning in relation to death, so what matters is burning brightly, like Tyrell's 'he who burns twice as brightly burns half as long' — he argues Joi becomes real by deleting her backup to live unguarded, 'like a real girl', and Deckard's 'I know what's real' names the responsibility and love for the daughter he has never met. K's arc, from Sapper's 'you've never seen a miracle' through Freysa's miracle birth to his mortal rescue of Deckard, shows realness is adopted through what one loves and dies for rather than conferred by origin.

S. Evan Kreider argues that aesthetic capacity evidences personhood in replicants: Kant's beautiful and the mathematically and dynamically sublime explain both K's cowed passage through Los Angeles and his storm-soaked defeat of Luv through strength of will and moral conviction. After Plato's and Aristotle's arousal and catharsis theories of art, he turns to Croce, Collingwood, and Suzanne Langer's expression theory and the 'virtual', reading Sapper's home-grown garlic, Joi's holographic dinner and rain scene, the Mariette-proxy sex as expressive symbol, and Stelline's memory-making ('we recall with our feelings') as aesthetic-emotional communication only persons can sustain. Even K's baseline judges personhood by the aesthetics of how he responds, not what he says.

Justin Kitchen uses the Stoic 'cradle argument' — Chrysippus on self-preservation, echoed in Wallace's 'the first thought tends to fear, to preserve the clay' — to deny that replicant slavery is natural, noting Seneca's point that rage like Batty's derails reason. Mapping the Stoic process of oikeiosis through Hierocles's concentric circles onto the films, he traces four stages: the Nexus-6's fight for survival, Rachael identifying with Deckard in love, the Nexus-8s' revolutionary community under Freysa, and finally K, who disobeys Freysa's order and sacrifices himself for Deckard as a Stoic cosmopolitan, a fellow citizen of the world. Replicants can become human because they develop through the same expanding circles of concern.
